cases.title: The “devil” you don’t know: A test of the detriments and benefits of co-founding with strangers
cases.method: Kickstarter founder survey (3,562 ventures); OLS, logistic/ordered/fractional models; coarsened exact matching

theory.claim: Co-founders who were previously strangers may add nonredundant networks, but uncertainty about trust and coordination creates operational costs.
theory.location: PDF pp. 2–3; “Stranger Puzzle” theory, H1 and H2
theory.source: Burt (2004) and Stinchcombe (1965) among cited supports
theory.comparison: Burt (2004): publisher bibliographic record located (DOI 10.1086/421787); existence only.

empirical.claim: Teams including strangers attract more external backers.
empirical.support: Authors report approximately 22% more backers after controls (reported b = 0.1972, p = .045).
empirical.location: PDF p. 10, results text; Table 4, PDF p. 11
empirical.comment: Reported association; not an independent calculation or causal assessment.

empirical.claim: The presumed skills advantage does not appear in the reported models.
empirical.support: Authors report no significant differences in breadth/depth of team skills, including the matched-model comparison.
empirical.location: PDF p. 10, results text; Table 5, PDF pp. 13–14
empirical.comment: Negative or null findings belong in the map alongside positive claims.

cases.title: Setting Higher Referral Targets Increases the Number of Women Recommended: Evidence From the Field and Lab
cases.method: Field and online experiments plus supplementary studies; OLS and mediation; N = 12,615 overall

theory.claim: Higher referral targets can motivate people to generate more referrals, increasing the number of women recommended.
theory.location: PDF pp. 2–3; goal-setting account and H1/H2
theory.comparison: Locke & Latham (2002): APA/PubMed bibliographic record located (DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.57.9.705); existence only.

empirical.claim: Requesting more referrals increases the number of women referred in Study 1.
empirical.support: Authors report 17% more women referred (mean .30 vs .26; b = .06, p = .03).
empirical.location: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 1511), hypothesis tests; Table 1 and Figure 2
empirical.comment: Source pointers aid retrieval; they do not validate the design.

empirical.claim: Prototype-divergence prediction is not consistently supported.
empirical.support: The field-study analysis reports an insignificant effect on the likelihood that a given referral is a woman (b = −.002, p = .90), with mixed evidence across settings.
empirical.location: PDF p. 8 (journal p. 1512), Study 1 results; abstract, PDF p. 1
empirical.comment: TRACE should preserve this qualification rather than flatten it into a blanket positive claim.

cases.authors: Li, Huang, Dineen, Wang, & van Jaarsveld (2025; online 2024)
cases.title: Voluntary Turnover Rate Fluctuations, Human Resource Practices, and Innovation: A Within-Organization Investigation
cases.method: Statistics Canada panel; 7,110 workplace-year observations across 1,980 workplaces; firm fixed-effects, quadratic terms and moderations
cases.file: Personnel Psychology - 2024 - Li - Voluntary Turnover Rate Fluctuations  Human Resource Practices  and Innovation  A.pdf

theory.claim: Complex adaptive systems reasoning predicts a U-shaped within-organization turnover–innovation relationship and shifts in its threshold due to HR practices.
theory.source: Nyberg & Ployhart (2013), Dooley (1997), and related theory
theory.comparison: Nyberg & Ployhart (2013): Academy of Management Review record located (DOI 10.5465/amr.2011.0201); existence only.

empirical.claim: A U-shaped within-workplace relationship appears in the main models.
empirical.support: Authors report linear B = −.38 and quadratic B = .88 (both p < .001) and state H1 is supported.
empirical.location: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 109), results; Table 2 (PDF pp. 9–10)
empirical.comment: Model coefficients are copied from author reporting, not re-estimated.

empirical.claim: HR practices shift the relationship’s estimated threshold.
empirical.support: Authors interpret employee participation and group-based pay as lowering the threshold, with individual-based pay raising it.
empirical.location: PDF p. 11 (journal p. 113), moderation results; Figures 2–4
empirical.comment: Evidence depends on interactions/curves, not a single coefficient or p-value.

cases.title: Do boards learn to hire? The effect of board experience with CEO replacement on CEO performance
cases.method: Longitudinal director/firm experience measures; 1,345 CEO successions in 900 firms; regression and robustness analyses
cases.file: Strategic Management Journal - 2025 - Boivie - Do boards learn to hire  The effect of board experience with CEO replacement (1).pdf

theory.claim: Rare, complex CEO hiring decisions can create superstitious learning instead of reliably improved selection.
theory.location: PDF pp. 3–6 (journal pp. 2469–2472), theory and H1
theory.comparison: Zollo (2009): INFORMS bibliographic record located (DOI 10.1287/orsc.1090.0459); existence only.

empirical.claim: More previous CEO-selection experience is associated with lower subsequent CEO performance.
empirical.support: Authors report b = −1.18, p = .01 in their main model and indicate support for H1.
empirical.location: PDF p. 13 (journal p. 2479), results; Table 3 (PDF pp. 16–17)
empirical.comment: Reported CiC-performance association; not an independent quality assessment.

empirical.claim: Domain-specific CEO hiring experience does not consistently offset the negative association.
empirical.support: Authors report H2a/H2b unsupported; reported strategic-similarity interactions b = −.43 (p = .29) and b = .22 (p = .57).
empirical.location: PDF p. 13 (journal p. 2479), H2 results; Table 3 (PDF pp. 16–17)
empirical.comment: Preserves failure to support proposed boundary conditions.
